market-equilibrium-s1.title: The market for cups of cocoa

table.caption: Cups of cocoa demanded and supplied each day at five prices at a winter fair (invented data for practice)

market-equilibrium-s2.title: A market after one curve shifted

market-equilibrium-s3.title: Two shifts at once in the blueberry market
market-equilibrium-s3.text: In the same summer, a widely shared study reports that blueberries are good for memory, and a late frost destroys part of the blueberry crop in the main growing region.

items.q: A popular study reports that eating oatmeal is healthy. Shift the right curve in the market for oatmeal and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: Tastes shift demand right. The new equilibrium is up and to the right along supply: a higher equilibrium price and quantity.

key.because: a change in tastes toward oatmeal

slips.S: The study changes what buyers want, so it shifts demand; oatmeal makers' costs are unchanged.

items.q: A drought destroys much of the orange crop. Shift the right curve in the market for orange juice and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: Supply shifts left along demand: the equilibrium price rises and the equilibrium quantity falls.

key.because: a drought that raises the cost of oranges, the input

slips.D: The drought changes what juice makers can offer, so it shifts supply, not demand.

items.q: Better robots cut the cost of making bicycles. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium in the bicycle market.

why.correct: Supply shifts right along demand: the equilibrium price falls and the equilibrium quantity rises.

key.because: a technology that lowers the cost of making bicycles

slips.D: Technology changes producers' costs, so it shifts supply.

items.q: The price of hot dogs, a complement, rises sharply. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium in the market for hot dog buns.

why.correct: Demand for buns shifts left along supply: the equilibrium price and quantity both fall.

key.because: a rise in the price of hot dogs, a complement

slips.S: Hot dogs are bought with buns by buyers, so their price shifts the demand for buns.

items.q: In the market for laptops, buyers' incomes rise (laptops are a normal good) and a new chip lowers the cost of making them. Shift both curves and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: Both curves shift right, so the equilibrium quantity rises for sure. The change in price depends on which shift is larger, so it is indeterminate without the sizes.

key.because: higher incomes and a lower cost of making laptops

items.q: Using the table, what is the equilibrium price of a cup of cocoa?

why.correct: At \$3 the quantity demanded (60) equals the quantity supplied (60).
options: At \$2, 75 are demanded but only 45 supplied.
Right: 60 demanded and 60 supplied.
At \$4, 75 are supplied but only 45 demanded.
At \$1, 90 are demanded but only 30 supplied.

items.q: Using the table, how large is the shortage at a price of \$2?

why.correct: A shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: $75 - 45 = 30$ cups.

mistakes.why: You added the two quantities. A shortage is the gap between them: 75 - 45.
You subtracted the wrong way. At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded is larger, so the shortage is 75 - 45 = 30.

items.q: Using the table, how large is the surplus at a price of \$5?

why.correct: A surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: $90 - 30 = 60$ cups.

mistakes.why: You added the two quantities. A surplus is the gap between them: 90 - 30.
That is the quantity demanded. The surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 90 - 30.

items.q: The fair sets the price of cocoa at \$4. What happens next in this market, if the price is free to change?
options: A surplus of 30 cups pushes the price down toward \$3
A shortage of 30 cups pushes the price up toward \$5
The market stays at \$4, because sellers set the price
A surplus of 30 cups pushes the price up

why.correct: At \$4, 75 cups are supplied and 45 demanded, a surplus of 30. Sellers with unsold cups cut prices until the market reaches \$3.
options: Right: unsold cups push the price down.
Above equilibrium there is a surplus, not a shortage.
With unsold cups, sellers compete by cutting prices.
A surplus pushes the price down, not up.

items.q: Cold weather arrives, and buyers now want 30 more cups at every price in the table. What is the new equilibrium price?

why.correct: The new quantities demanded are 120, 105, 90, 75 and 60. At \$4, 75 cups are demanded and 75 supplied.
options: At \$3, 90 would now be demanded but only 60 supplied.
At \$5, 90 would be supplied but only 60 demanded.
At \$2, 105 would be demanded but only 45 supplied.
Right: 75 demanded and 75 supplied at \$4.

items.q: Which curve shifted in the graph, and which way?
options: Supply shifted left
Demand shifted right
Supply shifted right
Demand shifted left

why.correct: The faded S1 lies to the left of the new supply curve, and demand has one position.
options: The new supply curve is to the right of S1, not the left.
Demand has one position in the graph.
Right: the new supply curve lies to the right of S1.
Demand has one position in the graph.

items.q: How did the equilibrium change in the graph?
options: The price rose and the quantity rose
The price fell and the quantity rose
The price fell and the quantity fell
The price rose and the quantity fell

why.correct: Supply shifted right down along demand: a lower equilibrium price, a larger equilibrium quantity.
options: That would follow a rise in demand.
Right: down and to the right along demand.
That would follow a fall in demand.
That would follow a fall in supply.

items.q: Which event could explain the change in the graph?
options: Several new firms enter the market
The price of a key input rises
Buyers' incomes rise for a normal good
A substitute good becomes cheaper

why.correct: More sellers raise the quantity offered at every price, shifting supply right.
options: Right: more sellers shift supply right.
A dearer input shifts supply left.
Higher incomes for a normal good shift demand, which stayed put.
A cheaper substitute shifts demand left, and demand stayed put.

items.q: What happens to the equilibrium price of blueberries?
options: It falls
It stays the same
It is indeterminate
It rises

why.correct: The study shifts demand right and the frost shifts supply left. Both push the price up, so the price rises for sure.
options: Neither shift lowers the price.
Both shifts push the price the same way.
When both shifts push price the same way, the price change is certain.
Right: both shifts raise the price.

items.q: What happens to the equilibrium quantity of blueberries?
options: It rises
It falls
It is indeterminate without the sizes of the shifts
It stays the same

why.correct: Higher demand pushes quantity up and lower supply pushes it down. Which wins depends on the sizes of the two shifts.
options: That holds only if the demand shift is the larger one.
That holds only if the supply shift is the larger one.
Right: the two shifts pull quantity in opposite directions.
That holds only if the shifts exactly offset.

items.q: What extra information would tell you whether the quantity of blueberries sold rises or falls?
options: Whether the price of blueberries rises
Whether the increase in demand is larger or smaller than the decrease in supply
How many growers live in the region
Whether blueberries are a normal good

why.correct: Quantity rises if the demand shift is larger and falls if the supply shift is larger.
options: The price rises in either case, so it does not settle the quantity.
Right: the relative sizes decide it.
The number of growers alone does not give the size of the supply shift.
The study shifted demand through tastes; income plays no part here.

items.q: A city holds the price of parking below its equilibrium level. What does the market show?
options: A shortage: drivers want more spaces than are offered
A surplus: more spaces are offered than drivers want
Equilibrium, because the city set the price
A shift of demand to the left

why.correct: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied: a shortage.
options: Right: too low a price leaves more wanted than offered.
A surplus comes from a price above equilibrium.
Setting a price does not make quantities match.
The price is on the axis, so the curves stay put.

items.q: Make the explanation specific: at the current price, buyers want more of a good than sellers offer. Fill in each blank.

why.correct: A shortage pushes the price up, which lowers the quantity demanded and raises the quantity supplied until the market clears.

specific.frame: There is a ___, so the price ___; as it does, the quantity demanded ___ and the quantity supplied rises until they are equal.

concept.label: What the market has
options: shortage
surplus

why.1: A surplus means more is offered than wanted; here more is wanted than offered.

price.label: The price
options: rises
falls

why.1: Buyers compete for the scarce units, so the price is bid up, not down.

change.label: Quantity demanded
options: falls
rises

why.1: A higher price lowers the quantity demanded, by the law of demand.

specific.model: There is a shortage, so buyers bid the price up because there are not enough units; as the price rises, the quantity demanded falls and the quantity supplied rises until the two are equal at equilibrium.

items.q: Which events would lower the equilibrium price of wheat, other things equal? Select all that apply.
options: A new seed raises the wheat harvest per acre
A drought cuts the wheat harvest
Bakers want more wheat to meet a rise in bread sales
The price of fertilizer, an input, rises

why.correct: Only a rise in supply or a fall in demand lowers the equilibrium price. The new seed shifts supply right; each other event shifts supply left or demand right, which raises the price.
options: Right: higher yields shift supply right, lowering the price.
A smaller harvest shifts supply left, raising the price.
More wheat wanted shifts demand right, raising the price.
A dearer input shifts supply left, raising the price.
